svg.text: Base shapes: one block, one edge length, two rest states
Every working edge (face F, laterals R and L) is exactly one unit long, so any edge can bond to any edge. Larger forms come from combinations and sequences.
A. The block family (a state, not a type)
K back (structure seed) — shrinks, gone in the triangle
The switch is a local state (like the core fold rule, or the programmable kind):
the laterals tilt and the back shrinks; F, R and L never change length. Chains turn only in 60° steps.
B. Bigger parts are bonded combinations (and can be split)
Edge-to-edge bonds pinned at both corners are rigid; one corner would make a hinge.
C. Sequence → shape: a chain folds into the shape its letters encode
While a letter is face-paired (being copied) it rests as a square, so copying stays straight and shape-agnostic.
Once free, each letter takes its encoded rest shape (dot: teal = square, amber = triangle) and the released strand folds.
SSS TTT SSS → hairpin (back to back)
Faces (orange) always end up on the convex side: a folded chain
keeps its copying faces exposed to the outside, like the half-cell.
Same sequence → same shape, so shape is inherited;
a copying error in the shape letter changes the fold.
